## NGO Website Development in India: Building a Donation Site That Works for Donors on Slow Phones

A donation website that loads slowly, shifts around while loading or fails on a weak connection loses donors at the exact moment they were ready to give. In NGO website development in India, the practical answer is to design for the hardest realistic visitor: a donor on a mid-range Android phone, on a patchy mobile network, possibly in a small town or on a train, who has perhaps a minute of attention and has just been moved by a WhatsApp forward or a field story. If your donate page works well for that person, it works for everyone. This guide explains how to build for that visitor, what to measure, and which decisions a trustee can make without knowing code.

It covers page weight, images, fonts, forms, payment flow, offline resilience and testing. It does not cover donation compliance such as 80G or FCRA, which we handle separately in [80G compliant donation platforms](/blog/80g-compliant-donation-platform-india) and [FCRA payment gateway setup](/blog/fcra-payment-gateway-setup-ngos).

### Who the donor actually is

NGO teams typically test their site on office broadband and a recent phone. Donors do not. Think of three common situations:

- **The forwarded link.** A supporter shares your campaign in a WhatsApp group. The recipients open it in WhatsApp's in-app browser, on whatever phone and network they have, and decide within seconds whether to stay.
- **The event follow-up.** After a fundraising event or a talk, attendees scan a QR code on a screen or a banner, usually indoors, where signal can be poor.
- **The returning donor.** Someone who gave last year and wants to give again quickly, on a phone they use for everything and with limited storage and memory.

None of these visitors will wait for a heavy page. They also will not tell you what went wrong. They simply close the tab.

## Start with what "fast enough" means

Google publishes thresholds for a good page experience, collected as the Core Web Vitals: Largest Contentful Paint (how quickly the main content appears) within 2.5 seconds, Interaction to Next Paint (how quickly the page responds when tapped) of 200 milliseconds or less, and Cumulative Layout Shift (how much content jumps around) of 0.1 or less, assessed at the 75th percentile of real visits ([web.dev](https://web.dev/articles/vitals)). Read that as three plain questions:

1. Does the page show me what I came for quickly?
2. When I tap Donate, does something happen right away?
3. Does the page stay still while I am about to tap?

The third matters more for donation pages than for most. Layout shift can make a donor tap the wrong amount, or nothing at all, when a late-loading banner pushes the button down. On a page that handles money, that is a trust problem as much as a usability one.

### Measure on the real device, not on the developer's laptop

Lab tools give useful estimates, and real-user data from Google's Chrome UX Report (shown in Search Console's Core Web Vitals report once you have enough traffic) shows what visitors experience. For an NGO site with modest traffic, field data may be sparse, so lean on lab testing with throttling: Chrome DevTools can simulate a slow mobile network and a slower processor. Better still, keep an inexpensive Android phone in the office and test on it, over mobile data, not Wi-Fi.

## Page weight: the biggest lever

Most NGO home pages are heavy because they are storytelling pages: large hero photographs, slideshows, impact counters, video embeds, partner logos, testimonials and a social feed. Each is defensible on its own. Together they can turn a page into several megabytes.

### Practical rules

**Set a page budget and hold the team to it.** Agree a target for the donate page and the top campaign pages, in kilobytes of transferred data, and treat exceeding it like exceeding a financial budget: something has to go. The exact number depends on your content, but a donate page should be far lighter than a home page, because it has one job.

**Make the donate page lean.** Remove the slideshow, the social feed and non-essential scripts from it. Keep a short reason to give, the amount choices, the form and trust signals such as your registration details.

**Delay what is not needed at first glance.** Anything below the first screen, such as a gallery, a map or an embedded video, can load later.

**Replace embedded video with a poster image.** A video embed pulls in a large player and scripts even if nobody presses play. Show a static image with a play button that loads the player only on tap. This alone can remove a lot of weight from a story page.

**Cut third-party scripts.** Each chat widget, analytics add-on, heat-mapping tool and social pixel adds requests and processing. Keep those you actively use and remove the rest. Ask every script's owner what decision it supports.

## Images: compress, size and serve sensibly

Photographs are the emotional core of an NGO site and also its most common speed problem.

- **Resize to the display size.** A photo displayed 400 pixels wide on a phone should not be delivered as a 4000-pixel original. Use responsive images so phones receive smaller files.
- **Use modern formats such as WebP or AVIF** where supported, with a fallback for older browsers. Most current platforms and build tools can do this automatically.
- **Compress with care.** Faces and expressions are the point of many NGO images, so check quality after compression. Modest, well-chosen compression usually preserves what matters.
- **Give every image dimensions** so the browser reserves space and the page does not jump as pictures load.
- **Lazy-load images below the fold, but not the first large image.** The main hero image should load promptly because it is what the visitor sees first.
- **Write alt text for meaningful images.** This helps screen reader users, and it also displays a description when an image fails to load on a weak connection. Our guide to [donor trust and website accessibility](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-accessibility-donor-trust-2026) covers this in more detail.

A note on sensitive images: field photography often involves children, patients or vulnerable people. Process images so metadata such as location is stripped before publication, and confirm consent covers online use. This is both an ethical and a legal point, particularly under India's data protection rules; see [donor and beneficiary data under the DPDP Act](/blog/ngo-donor-data-protection-dpdp-act-2026).

## Fonts and scripts

**Limit font files.** Every weight and style of a web font is a separate download. Two or three files are usually enough. If your audience reads Hindi, Marathi or another Indian script, choose a font designed for it and load only the scripts you need, and make sure the fallback font shows text immediately rather than leaving the screen blank while the web font loads.

**Prefer plain HTML and CSS where you can.** Effects such as animated counters and parallax scrolling need JavaScript that must download, parse and run on a phone with a modest processor. If an effect does not help a donor decide, drop it.

**Avoid heavy front-end frameworks for simple pages** unless there is a reason. A server-rendered donate page with a small amount of script will usually outperform a page assembled entirely in the browser on a slow device.

## The donation form: fewer steps, less typing

The form is where good pages fail.

### Reduce what donors must type

- **Ask only what you need to complete the donation and issue a receipt.** Name, amount, phone or email, and PAN only where an 80G receipt requires it and only when the donor asks for one.
- **Use the right input types.** A phone field should bring up the numeric keypad; an email field the email keyboard. Add autocomplete attributes so browsers can fill saved details.
- **Preset amounts as large tap targets**, with a clear "other amount" option. Where you can, tie amounts to a concrete outcome you can substantiate, for instance a defined cost your organisation actually incurs, rather than invented impact figures.
- **Keep the form on one screen where possible.** If you use multiple steps, show progress and keep entered data if the person goes back.
- **Show validation errors clearly, beside the field**, and never clear the whole form on an error.

### Make the payment step resilient

- **Offer the payment methods your donors use, prominently.** UPI is widely used in India, and a good donation flow lets donors pay through their installed UPI app without retyping details. Which methods appear, and what they cost you, is a separate decision that we discuss in [NGO payment gateway charges and settlements](/blog/ngo-payment-gateway-charges-settlements).
- **Handle interrupted payments.** On a weak connection, a donor may pay and then lose the confirmation page. Your system should reconcile on the server side through the gateway's webhook rather than relying on the browser returning to your thank-you page. Otherwise a donor may be charged with no receipt, or retry and pay twice. See [UPI donation reconciliation workflow](/blog/upi-donation-reconciliation-ngo-workflow).
- **Tell the donor what will happen.** "You will be redirected to your bank or UPI app and returned here" reduces panic and abandonment.
- **Send the receipt by email and WhatsApp** where the donor has agreed, so the confirmation survives a lost browser tab. Our guide to [WhatsApp donation receipts for NGOs](/blog/whatsapp-donation-receipts-ngos) explains the setup and consent rules.
- **Make retrying safe.** If a donor taps the pay button twice, your system should not create two charges. This is an engineering detail worth asking your developer about directly.

## Designing for interruption and weak connections

Mobile networks fail in the middle of tasks. A robust NGO site expects that.

**Cache the shell of the site.** A service worker can store core files after the first visit so returning donors see the page instantly, even on a poor connection. It needs careful setup: cache static assets, but never cache payment or personal data pages incorrectly, and ensure updates reach users.

**Show something useful when offline.** A simple offline page that says the connection is lost and offers to retry is better than a browser error.

**Keep pages functional without waiting for every script.** The core content and the form should work even if a non-essential script has not loaded. This "progressive enhancement" approach is a long-standing web practice that particularly benefits low-bandwidth visitors.

**Test inside WhatsApp's in-app browser.** Many campaign links are opened there. Some features that work in Chrome behave differently, so test your donate page through a link sent in WhatsApp.

## Hosting and delivery

Where your site is served from affects speed for visitors far from the server.

- **Use a content delivery network (CDN)** so that images, styles and scripts are served from a location near the donor. Many hosting providers include this, and it is one of the more cost-effective speed improvements.
- **Choose hosting with a server presence suited to India** for your traffic. If most donors are in India, a server far away adds delay to every request. Our comparison [WordPress hosting: shared, cloud and managed](/blog/wordpress-hosting-shared-cloud-managed) explains the trade-offs, and [choosing WordPress hosting in India](/blog/choose-wordpress-hosting-india) helps with the decision.
- **Enable compression** for text files, and caching headers so repeat visits are quick.
- **Prepare for spikes.** A media mention or a disaster appeal can bring in a great deal of traffic in hours. Confirm with your host how the site behaves under load and whether it can scale during an appeal.

## A worked example (illustrative)

Consider a hypothetical NGO campaign page built the usual way: a full-width slideshow of six large photographs, an embedded video, an animated counter, a live social feed, a chat widget, three analytics scripts and a donation form at the bottom. On an office laptop it feels fine. On a mid-range phone over mobile data, the donor sees a partly built page for several seconds, the slideshow shifts the content downward as it loads, and the donate button appears late.

A rebuilt version keeps the emotional core and drops the rest: one strong compressed hero image with reserved space, two or three sentences on why the appeal matters, a poster image in place of the auto-loading video, preset amount buttons, a short form and a registration line. The social feed and slideshow move to a separate stories page. The chat widget is replaced with a WhatsApp link. Analytics are consolidated into one tag.

We are not claiming a specific speed gain because it depends on the starting point, and we have not published measured figures for this example. The lesson is structural: the changes reduce work the phone has to do and protect the donation path.

## Testing checklist before you launch a campaign

1. Open the donate page on a mid-range Android phone over mobile data. Note how long until you can tap an amount.
2. Throttle the network in Chrome DevTools to a slow profile and repeat.
3. Check that the layout does not jump while loading.
4. Complete a real small donation using UPI and again using a card, and confirm the receipt arrives.
5. Interrupt a test payment halfway (close the tab after paying) and confirm your system still records it.
6. Open the link inside WhatsApp and inside Instagram's browser.
7. Run the page through Lighthouse and Search Console's Core Web Vitals report and note the biggest recommendations.
8. Check text is readable at a large system font size.
9. Turn on a screen reader briefly to make sure the form fields are labelled.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Why does my NGO website load slowly on mobile?

The usual causes are oversized images, embedded video, many third-party scripts, unoptimised fonts and slow hosting. A page that feels fine on office broadband can be very heavy on a mobile network. Testing on a real mid-range phone and running Lighthouse will usually point to the largest problems.

### How fast should a donation page be?

Google's guidance for a good experience is a Largest Contentful Paint within 2.5 seconds, an Interaction to Next Paint of 200 milliseconds or less and a Cumulative Layout Shift of 0.1 or less for most visitors. Aim to meet these on the donate page in particular, because it has the fewest reasons to be heavy.

### Do I need a separate mobile app for donations?

Usually not. A fast, well-built mobile website with a UPI-friendly payment flow serves most NGOs. An app is worth considering only if you have a clear need such as regular field-team workflows. We discuss the trade-off in [mobile app or mobile-optimised website](/blog/web-development-company-pune-mobile-app-vs-website-2026).

### Will a faster website raise donations?

A faster, simpler donation flow removes obstacles, but we cannot promise a specific increase, and none of the figures should be assumed for your organisation. Measure your donate-page conversion rate before and after changes and judge by your own data.

### Can WhatsApp campaign links be tracked?

Yes. Add tracking parameters to the links you share so your analytics can attribute donations to a campaign. Our guide to [NGO campaign attribution](/blog/ngo-campaign-attribution-fundraising) shows how to set this up.

## Where to Start

Take your current donate page and open it on the cheapest Android phone you can borrow, on mobile data, from a link inside WhatsApp. Time how long it takes before you can tap an amount and note anything that jumps or fails. That ten-minute test will tell you whether you have a problem and where.
